books.title: The Pinnacle of Reality
books.description: An Epic Tale of Reality and Destiny

pages.content:
The Realist sped across the street, narrowly avoiding an Itineror which swerved and broadsided into a streetlight. He vaulted over the rail protecting pedestrians from the roads and ducked behind a parked Itineror beside a transport parts shop.

The Itineror was an old model, and the large gas exhaust protruded crookedly from the underside. He crouched underneath this, trying to make himself as small as possible and blend into the drab grey color of the vehicle, matching his clothes. He breathed deeply, tired from the short chase. He was not old, but flashes of pain ran down the length of his body. So many scars…

Suddenly, the ground beneath him began to tremble. At that very moment, his head began to ache. This ache turned into a sharp pain that filled his mind, seeming to gnaw at his thoughts, scattering them. He must leave now, or he would weaken too much. But if he was exposed, out in the open, it would find him. The pain moved to wrap against his skull, and he groaned softly. With the consciousness that was left to him, he decided to leave the cover of the Itineror for somewhere else - anywhere where the unbearable waves boring into his head weren’t. He’d be quickly incapacitated otherwise.

He scrambled out from behind the Itineror on all fours, his thoughts all bent on how best to escape. But he couldn’t think, with energy draining out of him as the seconds passed. Then his gaze rested on the Itineror, and an idea sparked in his dulling mind.

He picked up a long metal pole lying beside him - the result of the Itineror which he’d barely avoided - and stabbed it into the narrow space between the door of the Itineror and its metal plating, hoping to use it as a lever to open the door. But his strength was fading fast, and his already weak attempts slackened. He ducked back behind the Itineror again. There had to be another way to do this, one that wouldn’t reveal himself.

But as he strained to concentrate, the air was filled with a sound. The sound of pistons, gears, and other mechanical parts, clicking to an unknown rhythm. It was coming closer, and with that realization, a strange calmness overcame him. He had no choice now, so there was no point in worrying.

Prologue: Shattered.content:

pages.content:
The mother was not surprised when something exploded two feet away from her, overwhelming her vision with the red and orange of fire, and she was thrown into an out-of-control spiral.

The wind screamed past her, the ground approaching, harsh and stern, her erratically flapping wings weak, grey and red blurring through her eyes. More wing flapping eventually allowed her to regain her balance, talons hitting the ground solidly, pain zinging up into her legs.

There were innumerable craters defacing the ground scattered around her, all a terrible witness to the death and destruction occurring. Each was filled with blood, death, decay: it was too much to bear thinking about. But she had to, for the sake of her egg, because her egg could be in any one of these.

And yet… it could be anywhere, even crushed under a dead dragon. But, in her heart, the life of the egg pulsed, tied to her. It had to be alive.

She tired and landed again, but once she had regained her strength she spread her wings and took off, flying low. She swept the ground with her eyes, scanning every grain for some sign of her egg.

As she headed closer and closer to the battle, the number of stray arrows and explosives increased. She hoped she could find her egg before — no, she couldn't, wouldn't think about that — wait. Why would the humans use arrows if they had explosives? Her thoughts were cut short when a volley of weaponry blasted towards her, arrows and debris flaming orange. She somersaulted and spun in response, letting herself be lost in the dance of the wind, just the once.

She landed - she needed to keep closer to the ground. The air was too exposed. A hiss. A rip. Then red hot blades slicing into her wing.

An arrow. The thought drifted across the haze of pain blanketing her mind, her vision filled with the black shaft. She took a breath, allowing the breeze to clear her head, steeling herself. She gripped the arrow in her teeth and wrenched it out. Her vision went red. She slumped, gasping, as the shaft clattered to the stones.

A fleeting glimpse of black blazing past. Then a heavy thud, thick and wet. She glimpsed scales behind her - but the dragon would be fine. An arrow alone could not kill a dragon. Then the arrow exploded.

Instantly the dragon was gone, vaporized.

She thought of the arrow which had hit her; if she hadn't removed it, she would be dead. Even as she looked back, the arrow detonated, creating another crater.

She began moving again, everything around her a mesh of dull grey, her wing dragging, scraping on the stones, just... moving.

She stumbled. The ground gave way beneath her - a flash of the sky - red, rushing towards her - a splash - and she was still. A cold liquid - blood, she realized, sloshed against her scales and her eyes cleared, taking in the grey walls of the crater around her. She brought her talons under her, pushing against the soft, murky ground, ignoring the searing stabs around her wing. She turned in a full circle, noting the steep, jagged walls, and realized she couldn't get out till she could fly.

Then, in the very center of the crater, she saw her egg. Her heart lifted, biting agony soothed, an energy thrumming through her as she reached for it, not noticing the arrow which slid into the water with barely a ripple, inches from her egg.

Then, the world exploded.

Commander-in-chief of the Royal Empire of the Fittus was fuming.

"Why were you worthless guards altering the formation? I clearly mentioned that you were not to change your formation, not even in the most dire of situations till I give the command!"

"But-"

The guard was not allowed to finish, because the commander-in-chief struck his chest. He did this with such force that the guard flew several feet before he fell to the ground, unconscious.

"Now," said the commander, "remove your unworthy selves from my presence. All of you." He spat on the ground and spread his wings, flying back to the underground cave system that was the home of all Fittus members.

But an irritatingly noble voice in his mind stopped him. At least you have a home, it said. Exploded suppressed a grunt — this voice was... right. He should be grateful. But his feelings still chafed underneath his scales.

He began to pace again. The commander was probably dealing with guards — perhaps, just this once, he would forget to call on Exploded. But he shook this thought off; he refused to give himself false hopes.

As he moved across the cave, the walls seemed to push in closer. He lifted his wings instead, taking off, denying the walls. Wind rushed at him, but he cleanly cut through, circling his cave. No matter what the commander planned for him - whatever happened - he would still have the freedom of flight. He would still lift his wings, deny the world, take to the sky.

The sky.

It was now that he wanted more than to be outside. Yet the commander only called on him after the time that Fittus members were allowed to fly free. True enough, guards monitored them at all sides - any attempt to escape would be severely punished - but still. The clear blues filled his mind, the thrill of speed, the calm greens of forest below. But the dark grey of the walls stood starkly against the blue - refusing to give freedom.

A small ache pulsed in the base of his wings - brought on by the demanding angle that his wings were forced at to fly in a sharp circle - and so he slowed, descending, at last alighting again on the stone floor.

From the passageway just outside the entrance to his cave, he heard the echoing clacks of talons that announced the coming of another dragon. A messenger, he decided, with a sinking of heart, that came to summon him to the commander’s cave. He slumped, wings falling slackly around his body. Despite all his efforts, he had hoped - and like always, he was disappointed.

He turned towards the entrance as a dark yellow dragon with splashes of black scales appeared.

“The commander summons you to his cave.”

Then the messenger was gone, turning curtly and disappearing down another passage. Suppressing a groan, Exploded exited his cave, turning into the familiar path - too familiar, even. He’d walked its length every day since he could remember.

Exploded stood hesitantly in front of the entrance to the commander’s cave. He knew he shouldn’t dawdle, but…

Enough. He should be braver than this. He stepped in.

Immediately, he straightened and assumed the position every Fittus member was taught when in the presence of the commander — wings tucked, head bowed, and every muscle locked into place. The commander's presence seemed to weigh on him, a cold pressure which made his scales prickle.

The commander's steps echoed as he circled slowly, each movement deliberate and predatory.

"Well, well," said the commander.

"I have summoned you here for an arrangement of power," he said, voice smooth, polished. "For countless years, the Fittus was governed under the same hierarchy — strength above all, lineage above strength, and tradition above both."

He paused behind Exploded, so close that the younger dragon felt the faint heat of his breath, sending shivers down his spine.

"Yet... following the ways of our forefathers is often the path to destruction. We must blaze a new path should we aim for true strength.

"Tradition rewards the loudest roars, not the sharpest minds. It crowns the largest wings, not the most capable claws."

Exploded swallowed. He was unsure how to act — should he agree or remain silent? But the commander gave him no time to decide.

He stepped into view again, wings half-spread. Not a gesture of threat, Exploded thought, but it wasn't comforting either. Something about the posture implied absolute dominance and control.

"I have watched brilliance buried beneath nobility; potential wasted because law demanded it."

The commander's tone changed slightly. Still cool and calm, but an added hint touched his voice, and his eyes narrowed slightly, black and depthless. His next words were spoken with a strange finality to them.

"I will not allow the Fittus to crack under the weight of its own arrogance."

Exploded's heart hammered. What did the commander want from him?

"From this day forward," the commander continued, "rank will be earned through trials — real deeds. Hunts, missions, and trials that reveal who a dragon is, not who tradition claims they should be."

The commander began to pace again, tail sweeping the stone floor with a soft scrape. "Dragons of cunning will face cunning. A dragon of strength will face claws and wings to rival them. Each dragon will face what they excel at."

Exploded found himself agreeing with the commander; he, too, did not find the hierarchy fair. So he dared a glance upward. The commander's expression was still neutral; neither cruel, nor kind, but calculating.

"These tests will not be announced," the commander said. "They will not be explained, nor questioned."

"The others will believe the trials are natural. Let them. Ambition grows best when it believes it is unseen."

Exploded made to speak, then stopped himself. Why was the commander telling him this, anyway? How was he special or different?

The commander's gaze suddenly fixed on Exploded, pinning him to where he stood. You wonder why I tell you this," the commander murmured. "It is because new blood adapts fastest. You are young. Unshaped. And… Hungry."

Exploded's breath caught. He had never been addressed so directly - and he had never spoken the question aloud. A cold chill set in, and he felt his scales shifting, clicking together quietly. Something was missing.

The commander stepped closer, staring at Exploded directly in the eye. Exploded wanted to look away, but the commander's eyes pulled him into their fathomless depths.

"If you are worthy, you will rise. You will fall if you are not. And only you will know that the trials are chosen — not random. Carry this knowledge carefully. Power is sharp - when mishandled, it cuts.”

The commander dismissed Exploded with a flick of his tail.

"You may leave."

A thrilling hum rushed through him as he turned, the caves around him melting together as he rushed through them. But his thoughts scattered and gusted before he could catch them, cool relief fighting with agitation bubbling up inside of him.

Words flitted through his mind — who was he, anyway? Why did the commander need him, in the first place?

But he couldn't organize and follow the thoughts. They rushed around him in waves. Had the commander really spoke to him? Addressed him directly? Revealed... secrets? He felt the taunting tinge of the last piece. Something that would fix it all.

Did he want strength? Did he really want position? Did the commander want... equality? The conclusion grew stronger. He forced himself to concentrate. But an energy thrummed through his mind, shattering his focus.

Lying. The commander was lying. No — Exploded was lying. To himself. A dream? Trust — he couldn't trust himself. Or the commander. Or... anything. Nothing was real.

Exploded felt jagged rocks underneath his talons. Bright light stabbed into his eyes, harsh red and slate grey refracting across his vision. Was all a dream, and this the reality? Craters. All around him. Deep gouges in the ground. Heat. Fire. Blazing red and orange. He didn't want this. He wanted the dream. The safe, stone caverns. Not this. He had to escape. He had to fly. He had to move. His wings wouldn't lift. His eyes wouldn't close. And the screams... agony echoing in his ears. Burrowing. Pain. A command. A noise. A flash. Brilliance. The world an inferno. Too much. His wings lifted — slowly, sluggishly, heavy. His surroundings blurred. Brightened. Disappeared.

Soft glowslug light danced around him.

A cold wind searched hungrily through the forest, swaying branches and shoving leaves aside. It bit into the rough bark of an oak, curling around the roots, then funneled underground. It blasted through the tiny opening, hissing through the crevices which pockmarked the hollow.

At last, the wind scraped along the rough, scarred scales of the dragon inside. A slight growl built in the back of his throat, a deep rumble which filled the hollow. A hesitant sliver of light crept through the opening, falling onto his eyes. A flash of scales - a metallic gleam - and the drag was upright, wings spread threateningly, ears swiveling.

Only the low groan of a tree bending against the wind, the crunch of dirt under a raccoon’s paw reached him. Slowly, his wings lowered, curving protectively around his body, and his jaw untensed. Tentatively, he lifted his wings, beating them gently until his talons no longer touched the ground. Tilting his snout upwards, he narrowed his eyes, angled his wings sharply, and shot upwards, the air hissing softly around him.

His claws locked into the groove of a stone inches above his snout, wings beating furiously to keep him aloft. He shoved his shoulders against the slab, heaving it upwards. With a final burst of effort, he lunged out of the hollow, his talons sinking into the damp forest undergrowth. With a slight shove he pushed the rock back into the opening, then turned to face skyward. Bending his forelegs, he launched off the ground, easily clearing the treetops, soaring as high as he could.

The winds played around him, their soft touch wrapping around him, relaxing his muscles. But he forced himself to tense. Even here, where not many dragons flew, he was never truly safe.

The air sharpened, cold, now stabbing into his lungs like claws as he gasped breath after breath. The muscles at the base of his wings vibrated with stress, keeping his wings aloft to slice through the currents. He angled his head downwards, scanning for movement below.

A brief moment—a flash of red quills cutting through deep green—and he folded his wings, streamlining his body, angling downwards, feeling the air screaming past his snout. Green leaves filled his vision, scratching, tearing at his scales as he cut through the forest canopy. Then the warm taste of blood, and the feel of the dirt beneath his claws, as he stood with the quill varg’s neck clamped between his jaws.

He shoved the creature over with a talon, ripped a few mouthfuls from its belly, and dragged it roughly behind a bush, staining it with blood. He turned back toward his hideout, but hesitated. He couldn't stay exposed for much longer—he'd be seen. Yet his wings screamed for the open sky. With a low grunt of frustration, his body betrayed his caution; he found himself launching off the ground, turning hard away from the den. If he covered enough distance, he could throw anyone tracking him off the scent.

A thrill rushed through him, sunlight refracting brilliantly across his scales, and he felt... free.

Then a sharp hiss. Cracking through the rush of the wind. "You...."

Frigid ice blasted through his veins. His wings seized. Slate grey scales flashed across his vision. Then he was flying—upwards. Ignoring the roaring wind. The tremor in his muscles. Higher. Faster. The wind burned at his throat, buffeted his body.

Then.... the air-rivers. The air threw him forward, wings shaking from stress, cutting through the sky. Yet he felt the scraping brush of teeth against his tail; the grey flashing in and out of his vision.

A sharper snap—the grey vanished—a jolt of white-hot pain—and he forced his wings to angle down, fighting the crushing pressure until the air-river finally released him. He dove downwards, a deep gash in the orangish stone growing wider. The color grew sharper—the light blazing off the walls—and he was in.

Then a solid wall. Color filled his view, his heart hammering against his ribs. With a roar, he flared his wings and snapped his body upright, breasting the wind. A blast of sparks, his wingtips scraping against stone—then he swung around the bend. The canyon floor rushed up to meet him, his legs jarring hard against the rock as he dropped.

He took a breath, then hurled himself forward, wings spread, rocketing through the tight trench walls. The canyon air battered his chest, but he gritted his teeth, slicing through, wingtips scraping stone. An ache at the base of his wings. A deep throb. He didn’t care. He didn’t slow.

A savage crunch behind him. A swirl of dust - a crack of stone. A screech, sparks flashing against the orange rock. Then the roar - a sound of fury, pain, reverberating through the trench. Ragged wingbeats, matching his own.

A hint of grey flashed behind him. He heard the ragged breaths. The pained wingbeats. His own heart thundered against his chest. The canyon suddenly swerved. But he was already banking to the left, smoothly cutting around the corner. A hiss of air, and the grey grew clearer. Closer.

He dropped suddenly, claws barely brushing the ground. A grey streak flashed above him, flipping the air, talons scraping stone, diving towards him. But he was moving - careening through the tunnel, pulling his wings back. Behind him, the slate blur grew larger. The gleam of scales, the flash of teeth filling his view. Heavy, ragged breaths.

Kill. He had to kill his attacker. There. A bottleneck.

A slight swerve to the right - into the bottleneck - and the light was gone. His wings pressed painfully close to his body, tucked almost pressing against his ribs. Only speed carried him now. A tremor in the air - a scrape at his tail - told him the attacker had followed.

A flare of light, from somewhere ahead. A sharp orange circle of stone: the exit. Narrow. Too narrow, almost.

Now. The spin.

He pinned his wings to his body. Sky and stone blurred around him. He extended his wings ever so slightly - catching the wind. Too late. His right wing caught, jagged rock ripping flesh and bone. Then air was rushing around him, the brilliant blue sky above.

Just behind - a sickening crunch, the screech of shredding scales against stone. A burst of rock and dust that billowed around him. A spray of crimson painted the stone.

The dragon turned, spreading his wings gingerly, one bent awkwardly. He flew low to the treetops, but quickly. Where there was one, there were always more.

There. His kill lay somewhere to his left; he smelled the fresh blood. He banked sharply, cutting through an opening in the treetops, landing softly. Noiselessly.

He couldn’t carry it. The realization forced him to bite back a low growl. His wing wasn’t strong enough to carry his prey. He’d have to stay in his den for… how many days, he didn’t know, before it healed.

But one thing burned clear inside of him - he, and all of the Unnamables, would have their revenge.

The light of the exit loomed ahead, and Exploded hurried his pace. Perhaps he’d make it without…

But a smooth, effortless click of claws against stone made him snarl softly into the darkness. A dragon with brilliant sapphire scales, shimmering softly with gold as the light reflected off her massive wings, swept out of a passage to his left.

Exploded folded his wings to his body, forcing his snout down and his tail around his legs, stepping to the side of the tunnel and up against the wall. The cold marble of a noble etch burned into his scales.

As the dragon passed, Exploded heard a hissed command - “Five fish from you, worker.” He felt his snout twist into a scowl, shoulders stiffening.

A rush of stale air as the dragon passed. Exploded crossed the rest of the way to the exit, the words still echoing inside his mind. But as soon as the light hit him, his expression relaxed, and the open sky called to him. He lifted his wings, and…

He was flying. Free. The dull grey of the Fittus receded behind him, and he flipped in the air with joy, feeling the sunlight warming his scales.

A slight tingle in his eyes, as the light reflected off them. Then snapping into view were the brilliant blue line of his Lodesight, running straight and parallel and combining into a brilliant blue beacon far ahead of him, the planet’s ancient gift of guidance to dragons. He turned leeward - opposite to the direction of the beacon - where the hunting grounds were. But the vibrant greens of the forest only reminded him why he was here, the thought weighing on his wings.

Even when he was outside, he wasn’t truly free. Guards - hundreds - surrounded the perimeter of the Fittus territory, and even though he could fly, it was for the nobles. A dragon’s only freedom - the freedom to fly - was the very thing that fed his imprisonment. Exploded flapped slowly towards the forest ahead.

Soon, the earthy tones were replaced entirely by a blur of green. A breath of the air—sweetened by the crushed pine needles he scented below—and his muscles threatened to relax, his stiff posture melting.

No. He gave a sharp shake of his horns, hissing softly into the wind. Focus.

He narrowed his eyes against the glare. A clear, glassy surface, threading through the green canopy. Exploded dove, wings folded against his body, air screaming past his snout, eyes slitted. Blue filled his vision. A hint of mist. Then—he spread his wings, leveling out, talons shearing through the water, twin sprays soaking his scales.

A violent jerk. The gleam of the sun—a flash of brown—and cold mud oozed into his scales. He took a sharp breath, a wet gasp that filled his nostrils with dirt.

A sharp ache at the base of his wing, twisted beneath him. He rolled himself, gasping, choking out the dirt that clogged his airways. He could taste the grit, wet and salty as it rested on his tongue.

Exploded forced his talons beneath him, scraping through the muck, and...

He could hear the cold hiss again. “Five fish from you, worker.”

A burst of strength. The mud sucked wetly as he forced himself upright, his twisted wing unfolding with a sharp slap. He spat the mud from his maw, and folded his wings onto his body. Or… he tried to. They slapped against him with a wet thud, the muck-caked surface rubbing awkwardly against his scales. He stumbled, slogging the few steps through the thick mud to the bank of the lake.

His breath rippled the surface, blurring the wet-scales which hid underneath. So he forced himself to exhale shallowly, gently through his nostrils. In the distance, a forest bird called. A sharp, piercing cry that cut through the soft hush of leaves in the wind. He heard the rapid beats of small wings, and he glanced upwards, catching a flash of the bird silhouetted against the light.

Free.

His throat seized up, and the rhythm of his breathing faltered. But he forced his glance away, focusing on the shallow breaths. The water stilled, revealing rich oranges and reds of the river stones, blanketed softly by swaths of dull green river-slime. The current rippled the color slightly, blending beams of light with the river bed.

A sapphire gleam of scales. Brilliant blue, shimmering softly gold. A wet-scale. Its tail end flicked gracefully as it glided smoothly through the water. And Exploded was no longer surrounded by bright forest. His vision was locked onto the scales, the blue and gold, as they passed him through dark tunnels, hissing at him. “Five fish from you, worker.”

Exploded snapped. He was no longer pressed against the wall, submitting—his claws slashed wildly at the scales, and…

His claws slammed against the cold stone, shock spearing through his leg, rattling his shoulder. Cold liquid swirled around, grey bleeding to blue, and he was looking into the depths of the water, claws dug into the river stone, the wet-scale… gone.

Exploded growled, the drying mud digging into his chest scales. He pulled his talon from the water, shoving it deep into the muck instead, the cool wetness soothing the pain.

He couldn't lose control again. So he closed his eyes, breathing deeply, shutting the hiss, the command, from his mind. He was catching wet-scales because he wanted to.

He stiffened his muscles, crouching at the water's edge, freezing his posture, one talon raised to strike. Controlled, shallow breaths barely stirred his chest as he waited. But one word lingered in his mind. Fish. He almost spat with disgust. The gliding, elegant way the word sounded from the noble's tongue, compared with the rough grunt of wet-scales.

No. Focus.

He stiffened his muscles, crouching at the water's edge. His wings were flared for balance, tail curling securely around a protruding root, one talon raised to strike. Controlled, shallow breaths barely stirred his chest as he waited.

He could feel the soft thrum of the water as it rushed over his claws, dug into the mud. The soft, musty hint of river-slime brushed his nostrils, the cries of distant birds reaching him. He still heard the voice, from long ago. The soft, rasping hiss scraping past an ancient dragon's throat. “Water is life for its creatures. It hides them. Trust not your eyes.” He could not strike at them, but just behind.

A sharp glimmer, off the water's surface. Again, sapphire and gold scales. He didn't hesitate. A sharp exhale; his claws sliced through the water, liquid dragging heavily against his forearm. The scraping brush of scales, but his claws dug deeper, piercing flesh. Foam, blood erupted. The wet-scale thrashed, whipping its body, loosening his claws. Its rough fins rubbed abrasively against his webbing.

Inhale. He drew his talons sharply out of the water, tail contracting around the serrated bark of the root, shifting weight to his back talons. He threw the writhing form onto the stone with a heavy smack, its tail still slapping against the stone. But the gleam of its scales dulled, its movement slowing.

The thrill of the catch rushed through him - an alive hum beneath his scales that made him shift his gaze eagerly back to the stream.

The only victory you've won is for the nobles.

The thought sliced through the glow of his joy, the dull scales of the fish mocking him. He slouched again, wings loose against his ribs, talons digging angrily into the quickly drying sand, glaring at the calmly rippling water.

The warm, rich taste of blood coated his tongue as his teeth cut into the quill-varg’s neck, snout stinging from the gashes its quills had sliced. He growled in grim satisfaction, allowing its lifeless body to drop next to the pile of fish.

Lush foliage surrounded him where he stood, in a roughly oval-shaped clearing. The quill-varg had been elusive in the thick trees - and its quills were difficult to evade when he attacked. So he’d forced it into this clearing, where he’d killed it from above.

Exploded turned from the carcass, heading towards the trees again. Just outside the clearing, the trees weren’t nearly tall or thick enough, so he was deep into the forest again before he found what he was looking for: A damp, large log roughly half his height. He sank his teeth into the bark, feeling its bitter grit scrape his tongue as he ripped away several large pieces.

Gripping them carefully in his teeth, he went back to where the carcass was, lying in a pool of its maroon-colored blood.

He pressed a piece of the bark onto its quills with an impatient talon. It was so unfair! The nobles were so weak, they couldn’t remove a quill-varg’s quills on their own! Why did they deserve respect? How did they earn the right to rule and control?

Traitorous thoughts. He pushed them to the back of his mind.

The quill-varg clamped firmly between his teeth, Exploded flew back towards the Fittus, Lodesight guiding him. He flew loomwards this time - opposite to the rising sun - till he reached the main forest again, where he banked sharply, flying lodeward. But his thoughts were sharp irritations as he tried to concentrate, and he found himself almost tearing straight through the creature with his teeth as he futilely tried to bury his anger.

There. Hidden from view by a thick coat of foliage, the stark grey entrance to the Fittus was a deep, concave dent into the stone, with a tunnel cutting through it. Exploded angled his wings, descending to land near the entrance.

He might have enjoyed the rush of the wind as he sliced through it - might have soared and circled as he landed instead of a sharp descent. Not today.

Each step through the tunnels felt heavier than the last as he plodded through them, the rich taste of blood souring on his tongue as he moved, seeking the familiar marking - an elegantly pointed leaf sheathed in silver. When he found it, he almost spat in disgust, scales bristling angrily.

He took a breath of the stale air to calm himself - another - before he stepped inside the noble’s cave.

The dragon’s back was facing him as he silently let the quill-varg rest on the floor. Stiffly, he managed to lower his snout and fold his wings before backing quickly out of the cave. But he could not prevent the beginnings of a growl deep in his throat as he turned to leave.

Exploded crouched in the thick grass, casting a quick glance at the sun. Less than an hour left till the sun reached its zenith, and then he’d have to go hungry for the rest of the day.

He gritted his teeth at the thought. Not time.

A sharp rustle somewhere ahead of him. He tensed his muscles, bracing his back legs against the packed dirt, claws sinking into the earth. Peering through the undergrowth at the small clearing beyond, a hint of brown fur caught the edge of his vision.

He didn’t move. He slowed his breathing close to silence, matching it to the rhythm of the wind.

A flash of movement from the creature - landing directly in his field of vision. The light glinted off its tiny teeth as it nibbled on something.

Exploded exhaled sharply as he leapt, wings extending to hug the wind, angling his body, claws pointed. A second of thrill - sunlight dancing across his scales - then his back claws gripped earth, front claws clutching fur. His teeth speared into the creature's flesh, warm blood coating his tongue.

And this time, he could enjoy it.

“Why was he chosen? Others have more potential.” The second-in-command’s voice was strained, repressing bitterness that threatened to edge his voice.

The Commander, back turned to him, didn’t move. Not even a twitch of his ears to show he’d heard.

The second-in-command shifted uncomfortably, a slight rustle of scales that at least was not the oppressive silence that pressed down on him.

“Chosen? No one has been chosen.”

The Commander’s voice cut suddenly through the quiet. Words froze on the second-in-command’s tongue, breath inhaled to speak released sharply. No one?

“The test remains.”

The second-in-command’s eyes widened in understanding. Yet - “If they fail?” He knew what the Commander’s test meant only too well.

“They will not fail.”

The words were spoken flatly. As if it was a fact.

The second-in-command bowed his snout, turning to leave. There were preparations ahead.

Exploded shifted, feeling rough grit scrape against his scales. His wings were splayed on either side, damp from the moss which dotted his cave. He stared dully at the dim glowslug light, watching the creatures wriggle across the wall. From somewhere behind him, he heard the steady drip of water as it filtered through a slit in the ceiling. The sound echoed strangely throughout the cave, a hollow crack that wormed into his ears. He rested his snout on the ground, cold chafing against his scales as he curled his tail around his head to muffle the sound.

Prologue.content:
The mother was not surprised when something exploded two feet away from her, overwhelming her vision with the red and orange of fire, and she was thrown into an out-of-control spiral.

The wind screamed past her, the ground approaching, harsh and stern, her erratically flapping wings weak, grey and red blurring through her eyes. More wing flapping eventually allowed her to regain her balance, talons hitting the ground solidly, pain zinging up into her legs.

There were innumerable craters defacing the ground scattered around her, all a terrible witness to the death and destruction occurring. Each was filled with blood, death, decay: it was too much to bear thinking about. But she had to, for the sake of her egg, because her egg could be in any one of these.

And yet… it could be anywhere, even crushed under a dead dragon. But, in her heart, the life of the egg pulsed, tied to her. It had to be alive.

She tired and landed again, but once she had regained her strength she spread her wings and took off, flying low. She swept the ground with her eyes, scanning every grain for some sign of her egg.

As she headed closer and closer to the battle, the number of stray arrows and explosives increased. She hoped she could find her egg before — no, she couldn't, wouldn't think about that — wait. Why would the humans use arrows if they had explosives? Her thoughts were cut short when a volley of weaponry blasted towards her, arrows and debris flaming orange. She somersaulted and spun in response, letting herself be lost in the dance of the wind, just the once.

She landed - she needed to keep closer to the ground. The air was too exposed. A hiss. A rip. Then red hot blades slicing into her wing.

An arrow. The thought drifted across the haze of pain blanketing her mind, her vision filled with the black shaft. She took a breath, allowing the breeze to clear her head, steeling herself. She gripped the arrow in her teeth and wrenched it out. Her vision went red. She slumped, gasping, as the shaft clattered to the stones.

A fleeting glimpse of black blazing past. Then a heavy thud, thick and wet. She glimpsed scales behind her - but the dragon would be fine. An arrow alone could not kill a dragon. Then the arrow exploded.

Instantly the dragon was gone, vaporized.

She thought of the arrow which had hit her; if she hadn't removed it, she would be dead. Even as she looked back, the arrow detonated, creating another crater.

She began moving again, everything around her a mesh of dull grey, her wing dragging, scraping on the stones, just... moving.

She stumbled. The ground gave way beneath her - a flash of the sky - red, rushing towards her - a splash - and she was still. A cold liquid - blood, she realized, sloshed against her scales and her eyes cleared, taking in the grey walls of the crater around her. She brought her talons under her, pushing against the soft, murky ground, ignoring the searing stabs around her wing. She turned in a full circle, noting the steep, jagged walls, and realized she couldn't get out till she could fly.

Then, in the very center of the crater, she saw her egg. Her heart lifted, biting agony soothed, an energy thrumming through her as she reached for it, not noticing the arrow which slid into the water with barely a ripple, inches from her egg.

Then, the world exploded.

Ch. 1 | Command.content:
Commander-in-chief of the Royal Empire of the Fittus was fuming.

"Why were you worthless guards altering the formation? I clearly mentioned that you were not to change your formation, not even in the most dire of situations till I give the command!"

"But-"

The guard was not allowed to finish, because the commander-in-chief struck his chest. He did this with such force that the guard flew several feet before he fell to the ground, unconscious.

"Now," said the commander, "remove your unworthy selves from my presence. All of you." He spat on the ground and spread his wings, flying back to the underground cave system that was the home of all Fittus members.

But an irritatingly noble voice in his mind stopped him. At least you have a home, it said. Exploded suppressed a grunt — this voice was... right. He should be grateful. But his feelings still chafed underneath his scales.

He began to pace again. The commander was probably dealing with guards — perhaps, just this once, he would forget to call on Exploded. But he shook this thought off; he refused to give himself false hopes.

As he moved across the cave, the walls seemed to push in closer. He lifted his wings instead, taking off, denying the walls. Wind rushed at him, but he cleanly cut through, circling his cave. No matter what the commander planned for him - whatever happened - he would still have the freedom of flight. He would still lift his wings, deny the world, take to the sky.

The sky.

It was now that he wanted more than to be outside. Yet the commander only called on him after the time that Fittus members were allowed to fly free. True enough, guards monitored them at all sides - any attempt to escape would be severely punished - but still. The clear blues filled his mind, the thrill of speed, the calm greens of forest below. But the dark grey of the walls stood starkly against the blue - refusing to give freedom.

A small ache pulsed in the base of his wings - brought on by the demanding angle that his wings were forced at to fly in a sharp circle - and so he slowed, descending, at last alighting again on the stone floor.

From the passageway just outside the entrance to his cave, he heard the echoing clacks of talons that announced the coming of another dragon. A messenger, he decided, with a sinking of heart, that came to summon him to the commander’s cave. He slumped, wings falling slackly around his body. Despite all his efforts, he had hoped - and like always, he was disappointed.

He turned towards the entrance as a dark yellow dragon with splashes of black scales appeared.

“The commander summons you to his cave.”

Then the messenger was gone, turning curtly and disappearing down another passage. Suppressing a groan, Exploded exited his cave, turning into the familiar path - too familiar, even. He’d walked its length every day since he could remember.

Exploded stood hesitantly in front of the entrance to the commander’s cave. He knew he shouldn’t dawdle, but…

Enough. He should be braver than this. He stepped in.

Immediately, he straightened and assumed the position every Fittus member was taught when in the presence of the commander — wings tucked, head bowed, and every muscle locked into place. The commander's presence seemed to weigh on him, a cold pressure which made his scales prickle.

The commander's steps echoed as he circled slowly, each movement deliberate and predatory.

"Well, well," said the commander.

"I have summoned you here for an arrangement of power," he said, voice smooth, polished. "For countless years, the Fittus was governed under the same hierarchy — strength above all, lineage above strength, and tradition above both."

He paused behind Exploded, so close that the younger dragon felt the faint heat of his breath, sending shivers down his spine.

"Yet... following the ways of our forefathers is often the path to destruction. We must blaze a new path should we aim for true strength.

"Tradition rewards the loudest roars, not the sharpest minds. It crowns the largest wings, not the most capable claws."

Exploded swallowed. He was unsure how to act — should he agree or remain silent? But the commander gave him no time to decide.

He stepped into view again, wings half-spread. Not a gesture of threat, Exploded thought, but it wasn't comforting either. Something about the posture implied absolute dominance and control.

"I have watched brilliance buried beneath nobility; potential wasted because law demanded it."

The commander's tone changed slightly. Still cool and calm, but an added hint touched his voice, and his eyes narrowed slightly, black and depthless. His next words were spoken with a strange finality to them.

"I will not allow the Fittus to crack under the weight of its own arrogance."

Exploded's heart hammered. What did the commander want from him?

"From this day forward," the commander continued, "rank will be earned through trials — real deeds. Hunts, missions, and trials that reveal who a dragon is, not who tradition claims they should be."

The commander began to pace again, tail sweeping the stone floor with a soft scrape. "Dragons of cunning will face cunning. A dragon of strength will face claws and wings to rival them. Each dragon will face what they excel at."

Exploded found himself agreeing with the commander; he, too, did not find the hierarchy fair. So he dared a glance upward. The commander's expression was still neutral; neither cruel, nor kind, but calculating.

"These tests will not be announced," the commander said. "They will not be explained, nor questioned."

"The others will believe the trials are natural. Let them. Ambition grows best when it believes it is unseen."

Exploded made to speak, then stopped himself. Why was the commander telling him this, anyway? How was he special or different?

The commander's gaze suddenly fixed on Exploded, pinning him to where he stood. You wonder why I tell you this," the commander murmured. "It is because new blood adapts fastest. You are young. Unshaped. And… Hungry."

Exploded's breath caught. He had never been addressed so directly - and he had never spoken the question aloud. A cold chill set in, and he felt his scales shifting, clicking together quietly. Something was missing.

The commander stepped closer, staring at Exploded directly in the eye. Exploded wanted to look away, but the commander's eyes pulled him into their fathomless depths.

"If you are worthy, you will rise. You will fall if you are not. And only you will know that the trials are chosen — not random. Carry this knowledge carefully. Power is sharp - when mishandled, it cuts.”

The commander dismissed Exploded with a flick of his tail.

"You may leave."

A thrilling hum rushed through him as he turned, the caves around him melting together as he rushed through them. But his thoughts scattered and gusted before he could catch them, cool relief fighting with agitation bubbling up inside of him.

Words flitted through his mind — who was he, anyway? Why did the commander need him, in the first place?

But he couldn't organize and follow the thoughts. They rushed around him in waves. Had the commander really spoke to him? Addressed him directly? Revealed... secrets? He felt the taunting tinge of the last piece. Something that would fix it all.

Did he want strength? Did he really want position? Did the commander want... equality? The conclusion grew stronger. He forced himself to concentrate. But an energy thrummed through his mind, shattering his focus.

Lying. The commander was lying. No — Exploded was lying. To himself. A dream? Trust — he couldn't trust himself. Or the commander. Or... anything. Nothing was real.

Exploded felt jagged rocks underneath his talons. Bright light stabbed into his eyes, harsh red and slate grey refracting across his vision. Was all a dream, and this the reality? Craters. All around him. Deep gouges in the ground. Heat. Fire. Blazing red and orange. He didn't want this. He wanted the dream. The safe, stone caverns. Not this. He had to escape. He had to fly. He had to move. His wings wouldn't lift. His eyes wouldn't close. And the screams... agony echoing in his ears. Burrowing. Pain. A command. A noise. A flash. Brilliance. The world an inferno. Too much. His wings lifted — slowly, sluggishly, heavy. His surroundings blurred. Brightened. Disappeared.

Soft glowslug light danced around him.

Ch. 2 | Scarlet.content:
A cold wind searched hungrily through the forest, swaying branches and shoving leaves aside. It bit into the rough bark of an oak, curling around the roots, then funneled underground. It blasted through the tiny opening, hissing through the crevices which pockmarked the hollow.

At last, the wind scraped along the rough, scarred scales of the dragon inside. A slight growl built in the back of his throat, a deep rumble which filled the hollow. A hesitant sliver of light crept through the opening, falling onto his eyes. A flash of scales - a metallic gleam - and the drag was upright, wings spread threateningly, ears swiveling.

Only the low groan of a tree bending against the wind, the crunch of dirt under a raccoon’s paw reached him. Slowly, his wings lowered, curving protectively around his body, and his jaw untensed. Tentatively, he lifted his wings, beating them gently until his talons no longer touched the ground. Tilting his snout upwards, he narrowed his eyes, angled his wings sharply, and shot upwards, the air hissing softly around him.

His claws locked into the groove of a stone inches above his snout, wings beating furiously to keep him aloft. He shoved his shoulders against the slab, heaving it upwards. With a final burst of effort, he lunged out of the hollow, his talons sinking into the damp forest undergrowth. With a slight shove he pushed the rock back into the opening, then turned to face skyward. Bending his forelegs, he launched off the ground, easily clearing the treetops, soaring as high as he could.

The winds played around him, their soft touch wrapping around him, relaxing his muscles. But he forced himself to tense. Even here, where not many dragons flew, he was never truly safe.

The air sharpened, cold, now stabbing into his lungs like claws as he gasped breath after breath. The muscles at the base of his wings vibrated with stress, keeping his wings aloft to slice through the currents. He angled his head downwards, scanning for movement below.

A brief moment—a flash of red quills cutting through deep green—and he folded his wings, streamlining his body, angling downwards, feeling the air screaming past his snout. Green leaves filled his vision, scratching, tearing at his scales as he cut through the forest canopy. Then the warm taste of blood, and the feel of the dirt beneath his claws, as he stood with the quill varg’s neck clamped between his jaws.

He shoved the creature over with a talon, ripped a few mouthfuls from its belly, and dragged it roughly behind a bush, staining it with blood. He turned back toward his hideout, but hesitated. He couldn't stay exposed for much longer—he'd be seen. Yet his wings screamed for the open sky. With a low grunt of frustration, his body betrayed his caution; he found himself launching off the ground, turning hard away from the den. If he covered enough distance, he could throw anyone tracking him off the scent.

A thrill rushed through him, sunlight refracting brilliantly across his scales, and he felt... free.

Then a sharp hiss. Cracking through the rush of the wind. "You...."

Frigid ice blasted through his veins. His wings seized. Slate grey scales flashed across his vision. Then he was flying—upwards. Ignoring the roaring wind. The tremor in his muscles. Higher. Faster. The wind burned at his throat, buffeted his body.

Then.... the air-rivers. The air threw him forward, wings shaking from stress, cutting through the sky. Yet he felt the scraping brush of teeth against his tail; the grey flashing in and out of his vision.

A sharper snap—the grey vanished—a jolt of white-hot pain—and he forced his wings to angle down, fighting the crushing pressure until the air-river finally released him. He dove downwards, a deep gash in the orangish stone growing wider. The color grew sharper—the light blazing off the walls—and he was in.

Then a solid wall. Color filled his view, his heart hammering against his ribs. With a roar, he flared his wings and snapped his body upright, breasting the wind. A blast of sparks, his wingtips scraping against stone—then he swung around the bend. The canyon floor rushed up to meet him, his legs jarring hard against the rock as he dropped.

He took a breath, then hurled himself forward, wings spread, rocketing through the tight trench walls. The canyon air battered his chest, but he gritted his teeth, slicing through, wingtips scraping stone. An ache at the base of his wings. A deep throb. He didn’t care. He didn’t slow.

A savage crunch behind him. A swirl of dust - a crack of stone. A screech, sparks flashing against the orange rock. Then the roar - a sound of fury, pain, reverberating through the trench. Ragged wingbeats, matching his own.

A hint of grey flashed behind him. He heard the ragged breaths. The pained wingbeats. His own heart thundered against his chest. The canyon suddenly swerved. But he was already banking to the left, smoothly cutting around the corner. A hiss of air, and the grey grew clearer. Closer.

He dropped suddenly, claws barely brushing the ground. A grey streak flashed above him, flipping the air, talons scraping stone, diving towards him. But he was moving - careening through the tunnel, pulling his wings back. Behind him, the slate blur grew larger. The gleam of scales, the flash of teeth filling his view. Heavy, ragged breaths.

Kill. He had to kill his attacker. There. A bottleneck.

A slight swerve to the right - into the bottleneck - and the light was gone. His wings pressed painfully close to his body, tucked almost pressing against his ribs. Only speed carried him now. A tremor in the air - a scrape at his tail - told him the attacker had followed.

A flare of light, from somewhere ahead. A sharp orange circle of stone: the exit. Narrow. Too narrow, almost.

Now. The spin.

He pinned his wings to his body. Sky and stone blurred around him. He extended his wings ever so slightly - catching the wind. Too late. His right wing caught, jagged rock ripping flesh and bone. Then air was rushing around him, the brilliant blue sky above.

Just behind - a sickening crunch, the screech of shredding scales against stone. A burst of rock and dust that billowed around him. A spray of crimson painted the stone.

The dragon turned, spreading his wings gingerly, one bent awkwardly. He flew low to the treetops, but quickly. Where there was one, there were always more.

There. His kill lay somewhere to his left; he smelled the fresh blood. He banked sharply, cutting through an opening in the treetops, landing softly. Noiselessly.

He couldn’t carry it. The realization forced him to bite back a low growl. His wing wasn’t strong enough to carry his prey. He’d have to stay in his den for… how many days, he didn’t know, before it healed.

But one thing burned clear inside of him - he, and all of the Unnamables, would have their revenge.

The light of the exit loomed ahead, and Exploded hurried his pace. Perhaps he’d make it without…

But a smooth, effortless click of claws against stone made him snarl softly into the darkness. A dragon with brilliant sapphire scales, shimmering softly with gold as the light reflected off her massive wings, swept out of a passage to his left.

Exploded folded his wings to his body, forcing his snout down and his tail around his legs, stepping to the side of the tunnel and up against the wall. The cold marble of a noble etch burned into his scales.

As the dragon passed, Exploded heard a hissed command - “Five fish from you, worker.” He felt his snout twist into a scowl, shoulders stiffening.

A rush of stale air as the dragon passed. Exploded crossed the rest of the way to the exit, the words still echoing inside his mind. But as soon as the light hit him, his expression relaxed, and the open sky called to him. He lifted his wings, and…

He was flying. Free. The dull grey of the Fittus receded behind him, and he flipped in the air with joy, feeling the sunlight warming his scales.

A slight tingle in his eyes, as the light reflected off them. Then snapping into view were the brilliant blue line of his Lodesight, running straight and parallel and combining into a brilliant blue beacon far ahead of him, the planet’s ancient gift of guidance to dragons. He turned leeward - opposite to the direction of the beacon - where the hunting grounds were. But the vibrant greens of the forest only reminded him why he was here, the thought weighing on his wings.

Even when he was outside, he wasn’t truly free. Guards - hundreds - surrounded the perimeter of the Fittus territory, and even though he could fly, it was for the nobles. A dragon’s only freedom - the freedom to fly - was the very thing that fed his imprisonment. Exploded flapped slowly towards the forest ahead.

Soon, the earthy tones were replaced entirely by a blur of green. A breath of the air—sweetened by the crushed pine needles he scented below—and his muscles threatened to relax, his stiff posture melting.

No. He gave a sharp shake of his horns, hissing softly into the wind. Focus.

He narrowed his eyes against the glare. A clear, glassy surface, threading through the green canopy. Exploded dove, wings folded against his body, air screaming past his snout, eyes slitted. Blue filled his vision. A hint of mist. Then—he spread his wings, leveling out, talons shearing through the water, twin sprays soaking his scales.

A violent jerk. The gleam of the sun—a flash of brown—and cold mud oozed into his scales. He took a sharp breath, a wet gasp that filled his nostrils with dirt.

A sharp ache at the base of his wing, twisted beneath him. He rolled himself, gasping, choking out the dirt that clogged his airways. He could taste the grit, wet and salty as it rested on his tongue.

Exploded forced his talons beneath him, scraping through the muck, and...

He could hear the cold hiss again. “Five fish from you, worker.”

A burst of strength. The mud sucked wetly as he forced himself upright, his twisted wing unfolding with a sharp slap. He spat the mud from his maw, and folded his wings onto his body. Or… he tried to. They slapped against him with a wet thud, the muck-caked surface rubbing awkwardly against his scales. He stumbled, slogging the few steps through the thick mud to the bank of the lake.

His breath rippled the surface, blurring the wet-scales which hid underneath. So he forced himself to exhale shallowly, gently through his nostrils. In the distance, a forest bird called. A sharp, piercing cry that cut through the soft hush of leaves in the wind. He heard the rapid beats of small wings, and he glanced upwards, catching a flash of the bird silhouetted against the light.

Free.

His throat seized up, and the rhythm of his breathing faltered. But he forced his glance away, focusing on the shallow breaths. The water stilled, revealing rich oranges and reds of the river stones, blanketed softly by swaths of dull green river-slime. The current rippled the color slightly, blending beams of light with the river bed.

A sapphire gleam of scales. Brilliant blue, shimmering softly gold. A wet-scale. Its tail end flicked gracefully as it glided smoothly through the water. And Exploded was no longer surrounded by bright forest. His vision was locked onto the scales, the blue and gold, as they passed him through dark tunnels, hissing at him. “Five fish from you, worker.”

Exploded snapped. He was no longer pressed against the wall, submitting—his claws slashed wildly at the scales, and…

His claws slammed against the cold stone, shock spearing through his leg, rattling his shoulder. Cold liquid swirled around, grey bleeding to blue, and he was looking into the depths of the water, claws dug into the river stone, the wet-scale… gone.

Exploded growled, the drying mud digging into his chest scales. He pulled his talon from the water, shoving it deep into the muck instead, the cool wetness soothing the pain.

He couldn't lose control again. So he closed his eyes, breathing deeply, shutting the hiss, the command, from his mind. He was catching wet-scales because he wanted to.

He stiffened his muscles, crouching at the water's edge, freezing his posture, one talon raised to strike. Controlled, shallow breaths barely stirred his chest as he waited. But one word lingered in his mind. Fish. He almost spat with disgust. The gliding, elegant way the word sounded from the noble's tongue, compared with the rough grunt of wet-scales.

No. Focus.

He stiffened his muscles, crouching at the water's edge. His wings were flared for balance, tail curling securely around a protruding root, one talon raised to strike. Controlled, shallow breaths barely stirred his chest as he waited.

He could feel the soft thrum of the water as it rushed over his claws, dug into the mud. The soft, musty hint of river-slime brushed his nostrils, the cries of distant birds reaching him. He still heard the voice, from long ago. The soft, rasping hiss scraping past an ancient dragon's throat. “Water is life for its creatures. It hides them. Trust not your eyes.” He could not strike at them, but just behind.

A sharp glimmer, off the water's surface. Again, sapphire and gold scales. He didn't hesitate. A sharp exhale; his claws sliced through the water, liquid dragging heavily against his forearm. The scraping brush of scales, but his claws dug deeper, piercing flesh. Foam, blood erupted. The wet-scale thrashed, whipping its body, loosening his claws. Its rough fins rubbed abrasively against his webbing.

Inhale. He drew his talons sharply out of the water, tail contracting around the serrated bark of the root, shifting weight to his back talons. He threw the writhing form onto the stone with a heavy smack, its tail still slapping against the stone. But the gleam of its scales dulled, its movement slowing.

The thrill of the catch rushed through him - an alive hum beneath his scales that made him shift his gaze eagerly back to the stream.

The only victory you've won is for the nobles.

The thought sliced through the glow of his joy, the dull scales of the fish mocking him. He slouched again, wings loose against his ribs, talons digging angrily into the quickly drying sand, glaring at the calmly rippling water.

He pressed a piece of the bark onto its quills with an impatient talon. It was so unfair! The nobles were so weak, they couldn’t remove a quill-varg’s quills on their own! Why did they deserve respect? How did they earn the right to rule and control?

Traitorous thoughts. He pushed them to the back of his mind.

The quill-varg clamped firmly between his teeth, Exploded flew back towards the Fittus, Lodesight guiding him. He flew loomwards this time - opposite to the rising sun - till he reached the main forest again, where he banked sharply, flying lodeward. But his thoughts were sharp irritations as he tried to concentrate, and he found himself almost tearing straight through the creature with his teeth as he futilely tried to bury his anger.

There. Hidden from view by a thick coat of foliage, the stark grey entrance to the Fittus was a deep, concave dent into the stone, with a tunnel cutting through it. Exploded angled his wings, descending to land near the entrance.

He might have enjoyed the rush of the wind as he sliced through it - might have soared and circled as he landed instead of a sharp descent. Not today.

Each step through the tunnels felt heavier than the last as he plodded through them, the rich taste of blood souring on his tongue as he moved, seeking the familiar marking - an elegantly pointed leaf sheathed in silver. When he found it, he almost spat in disgust, scales bristling angrily.

He took a breath of the stale air to calm himself - another - before he stepped inside the noble’s cave.

The dragon’s back was facing him as he silently let the quill-varg rest on the floor. Stiffly, he managed to lower his snout and fold his wings before backing quickly out of the cave. But he could not prevent the beginnings of a growl deep in his throat as he turned to leave.

Exploded exhaled sharply as he leapt, wings extending to hug the wind, angling his body, claws pointed. A second of thrill - sunlight dancing across his scales - then his back claws gripped earth, front claws clutching fur. His teeth speared into the creature's flesh, warm blood coating his tongue.

And this time, he could enjoy it.

Ch. 3 | Infiltrate.content:
“Why was he chosen? Others have more potential.” The second-in-command’s voice was strained, repressing bitterness that threatened to edge his voice.

The Commander, back turned to him, didn’t move. Not even a twitch of his ears to show he’d heard.

The second-in-command shifted uncomfortably, a slight rustle of scales that at least was not the oppressive silence that pressed down on him.

“Chosen? No one has been chosen.”

The Commander’s voice cut suddenly through the quiet. Words froze on the second-in-command’s tongue, breath inhaled to speak released sharply. No one?

“The test remains.”

The second-in-command’s eyes widened in understanding. Yet - “If they fail?” He knew what the Commander’s test meant only too well.

“They will not fail.”

The words were spoken flatly. As if it was a fact.

The second-in-command bowed his snout, turning to leave. There were preparations ahead.

Exploded shifted, feeling rough grit scrape against his scales. His wings were splayed on either side, damp from the moss which dotted his cave. He stared dully at the dim glowslug light, watching the creatures wriggle across the wall. From somewhere behind him, he heard the steady drip of water as it filtered through a slit in the ceiling. The sound echoed strangely throughout the cave, a hollow crack that wormed into his ears. He rested his snout on the ground, cold chafing against his scales as he curled his tail around his head to muffle the sound.

Though he’d slept, the throb in his muscles still pulsed insistently, sending a wave of pain through his legs as he turned again. Exploded curved his wings back around his body, trying to keep the warmth in.

“Pointless,” he mumbled into his tail. Once the drafts started to blow… he grimaced at the thought. “But it’ll have to do.”

His tail vibrated with the rumble of his voice, sending a thrum through his horns, and he almost smiled at the sensation.

Almost.

“I’m talking to myself again,” he noted out loud. But then - who else to talk to? He was alone in his cave, and in these long hours, when he wasn’t on hunt duty… he had only glowslugs to keep him company.

The noble voice in his head piped up.

Exploded felt his tail begin to twitch where it rested against his jaw. “Like anyone would talk to me,” he told it.

It was silent for a moment.

Exploded growled.

The voice didn't bother him after that.

“Enough,” he told himself firmly. He glanced at the glowslugs - their light was beginning to fade. The messenger would arrive soon, and he needed to be ready. He stood, arranging his wings to rest around his ribs, jaw tensed.

Once every seven starrisings, the Fittus demanded he perform his most dangerous duty:

The night patrol.
